calls.reason: Federal Reserve research finds continued but slower coder employment growth; Anthropic reports reduced hiring alongside growing technical employment. These mixed signals do not settle replacement, and “soon” has no clear endpoint.

Nunes and colleagues found most attempted maintainability fixes introduced errors or new maintenance issues. Although the experiments predate publication and lack long-term follow-up, they support the main point that substantial maintenance difficulties remained.

The novice experiment shows poor repair performance after unreviewed AI use, and Veracode finds security flaws. Neither establishes that beginner overdependence produced substantial tangled code and security problems.

SWE-Lancer documents frequent engineering failures, while Anthropic reports stronger contemporary coding capabilities. Neither directly establishes continued dependence on human understanding across debugging, architecture, and client needs.

GovTech and Al Haque report perceived learning benefits, but direct API-learning evidence is thin. Anthropic’s later trial finds reduced average mastery, and the programming-language extension is explicitly tentative.

The statement is a rhetorical judgment without a deadline. Stanford finds declining employment for young developers but growth for older groups, which does not settle whether these occupations are becoming obsolete.
